The Quiet Craft of Japanese Joinery

In a small workshop on the edge of Kyoto, a carpenter named Hideo lays out a beam of hinoki cypress. He will not use a single nail. Instead, the timber will lock together through a sequence of cuts that have been refined over a thousand years, each one a small puzzle solved in wood.

Japanese joinery, known as sashimono for furniture and kigumi for buildings, relies on the natural movement of wood. Joints are cut so that they tighten as the seasons change, and a well-made temple can be dismantled, repaired and reassembled centuries later. Carpenters train for a decade before they are trusted with the most demanding joints.

The tools are simple: a pull saw, a set of chisels, a plane that is drawn toward the body rather than pushed. What is not simple is the patience. Hideo spends more time sharpening and measuring than he does cutting. "The wood tells you where it wants to go," he says, running a thumb along the grain. "You just have to listen long enough."

Today the craft faces a shortage of apprentices, but a new generation of designers has rediscovered it. Architects borrow the logic of interlocking joints for modern timber towers, and furniture makers sell flat-packed pieces that assemble without glue. The quiet craft, it seems, still has something to say.
